name: Mandible
func: The lower jaw bone, the largest and strongest bone of the face. It holds the lower teeth and moves at the jaw joints so you can chew, talk and swallow.

levels.kid:
Your **mandible** is your **lower jaw**. Put your hand under your chin and open your mouth: the bone that moves down is your mandible!

It's shaped a bit like a horseshoe, or the letter U. It holds all your bottom teeth.

The mandible is the only bone in your head that can really move. It's attached to the rest of your skull by two little hinges, one just in front of each ear. Put your fingers there and chew, and you can feel them sliding!

Strong muscles in your cheeks pull the mandible up so you can bite and chew crunchy apples. It also moves when you talk, sing, yawn and laugh.
levels.hs:
The **mandible** is the U-shaped lower jaw and the largest, strongest bone of the face. It is the only skull bone joined by a true movable joint.

Its parts are the curved **body**, which carries the lower teeth in sockets along the **alveolar process**, and two upright **rami** on each side. The body and ramus meet at the **angle** of the jaw, which you can feel below each earlobe. The front midline point of the chin is the **mental protuberance**.

At the top of each ramus are two projections: the **coronoid process** in front, where the **temporalis** muscle attaches, and the **condylar process** (condyle) behind, which forms the **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)** with the temporal bone just in front of the ear canal.

The mandible sits below the maxilla (upper jaw) and in front of the neck; the tongue and floor of the mouth sit inside its U. The **masseter**, **temporalis** and **pterygoid** muscles move it. A nerve runs through a canal inside the bone and supplies feeling to the lower teeth, then exits at the **mental foramen** to supply the chin and lower lip.
levels.college:
Key features:
- **Mandibular foramen** on the inner ramus, guarded by the **lingula**: the **inferior alveolar nerve** (branch of V3) and vessels enter here, run through the **mandibular canal** to supply the lower teeth, and exit as the **mental nerve** at the **mental foramen** (below the second premolar).
- **Mylohyoid line** on the inner body: attachment of the mylohyoid muscle, the floor of the mouth.
- **Genial tubercles (mental spines)**: attachments of genioglossus and geniohyoid.
- **Pterygoid fovea** on the condylar neck: attachment of the lateral pterygoid.

The **TMJ** is a synovial joint with an **articular disc** dividing it into upper and lower compartments. Opening starts with **hinge rotation** in the lower compartment, then the condyle and disc **glide forward** onto the articular eminence (upper compartment) for wide opening.

Muscles of mastication, all supplied by the **mandibular nerve (V3)**:
- Close: **masseter**, **temporalis**, **medial pterygoid**.
- Open and protrude: **lateral pterygoid** (with gravity and suprahyoid muscles).
- Retrude: posterior fibres of temporalis.

The **facial artery** crosses the lower border of the mandible just in front of the masseter, where its pulse can be felt. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs near the lower border.
levels.phd:
The mandible develops in the **first pharyngeal arch**. **Cranial neural crest** cells form the mesenchyme around **Meckel's cartilage**, a rod of cartilage that acts as a template. Most of the mandible forms by **intramembranous ossification** lateral to Meckel's cartilage rather than by replacing it; the cartilage's posterior end becomes the malleus and incus of the middle ear and the sphenomandibular ligament. This is why first-arch syndromes (e.g. **Treacher Collins syndrome**, from TCOF1 mutations disrupting neural crest ribosome biogenesis) affect both jaw and ear.

The **condylar cartilage** is a **secondary cartilage** that forms later and acts as an adaptive growth site, responding to mechanical load. Its cells come from a periosteum-like layer rather than a classic growth plate. Signalling via **Indian hedgehog**, PTHrP and SOX9 controls it, and this plasticity is what orthodontic functional appliances exploit.

Evolutionarily, the mammalian jaw is a single bone (the **dentary**); in reptiles, several bones form the lower jaw, and two of them became the mammalian middle ear ossicles, one of the best-documented transitions in the fossil record.

Masticatory forces are large: molar bite forces in adults can reach several hundred newtons. The mandible's cortical bone is thickest along the lower border and shows **trajectories** aligned with these loads. The jawbone around teeth remodels rapidly; after tooth loss, the alveolar ridge resorbs, which matters for dental implants. Bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis selectively affects the jaw, likely because of its high remodelling rate and thin overlying mucosa.
levels.expert:
**Mandibular fractures** are among the most common facial fractures. Because the mandible is a ring with the skull base, it often breaks in **two places** (e.g. a blow to one side fracturing the body there and the opposite condyle). Common sites are the **condylar neck**, **angle** (especially with an impacted wisdom tooth) and **parasymphysis**. Signs: malocclusion, pain, a step in the teeth, sublingual haematoma and numbness of the lower lip and chin from **inferior alveolar nerve** injury. Bilateral condylar fractures can produce an anterior open bite.

Imaging: an **orthopantomogram (OPG)** plus another view, or **CT** for complex injuries. Treatment in general is reduction and fixation with **titanium plates** or temporary wiring of the teeth together.

**TMJ dislocation** happens with wide yawning: the condyle locks in front of the articular eminence, and the mouth cannot close. It is reduced by pressing down and back on the molars.

The **jaw jerk** reflex (tapping the chin with the mouth slightly open) tests the trigeminal nerve and pons; a brisk jaw jerk suggests an upper motor neuron lesion above the pons, helping separate brain from cervical cord causes of spasticity.

The mandible is a surgical route too: a **mandibulotomy** (splitting the jaw) gives access to the back of the mouth and throat. In neurosurgery, the **trigeminal nerve**'s mandibular division (V3) is relevant to trigeminal neuralgia, which can cause electric pains along the jaw. The **marginal mandibular nerve** must be protected in neck incisions, or the lower lip droops.

keyPoints: Largest, strongest facial bone; only movable skull bone
Parts: body, ramus, angle, coronoid and condylar processes
TMJ: condyle + temporal bone with an articular disc; hinges then glides
Inferior alveolar nerve enters mandibular foramen, exits as mental nerve
Often fractures in two places because it forms a ring with the skull

test.q: Which part of the mandible forms the temporomandibular joint?
test.explain: The condyle sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone.

test.q: The nerve that gives feeling to the chin and lower lip exits the mental foramen. What is it called?
test.explain: The mental nerve is the end branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).

test.q: Which muscle mainly OPENS the jaw and pulls it forward?
test.explain: The lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disc forward onto the articular eminence.

test.q: All muscles of mastication are supplied by which nerve?
test.explain: The motor root of the trigeminal travels with V3.

test.q: A brisk version of which reflex suggests an upper motor neuron lesion above the pons?
test.explain: The jaw jerk's reflex arc is in the pons, so it separates lesions above the pons from cervical cord lesions.
